L50: Target contamination is the main problem in traditional target detection (TD) methods in hyperspectral imagery when estimating the background distribution with different models. Sparse approximation is introduced to tackle the detection problem, yet while using windows to build a sparse dictionary, the contamination problem remains. In our approach, we utilize a learning method based on convex optimization to build such a dictionary.
L51: Through its application, prior information such as the size of windows can be spared while considerably reducing the occurrence of contamination. To verify the efficacy of using the learned dictionary (LD), the dictionary built through the dual window (DW) method is used as a comparison, and two sparse TD methods are employed afterward. Experimental results show that, by using the LD, a better result is obtained compared with the methods using a traditional DW background dictionary.

L128: I. I NTRODUCTION
L129: 
L130: H YPERSPECTRAL imagery (HSI) contains valuable in-
L131: 
L132: formation about spectral characteristics compared with
L133: 
L134: other remote sensing images. As each pixel in HSI has hundreds
L135: 
L136: of continuous spectrums, the data structure of HSI is similar to a
L137: hypercube, each layer of which is a whole image of one speciﬁc
L138: 
L139: spectral band. Given the complexity of HSI, making full use of
L140: 
L141: these hypercubes has become the major challenge nowadays.
L142: 
L143: T arget detection (TD) is one of the most important appli-
L144: 
L145: cations, which is a kind of binary classiﬁcation that labels a
L146: 
L147: pixel on HSI as a target or a background based on its spectrum.
L148: 
L149: T o utilize the abundant spectral characteristics of HSI, a great
L150: 
L151: number of traditional TD methods such as constrained energy
L152: minimization (CEM) and the adaptive coherence/cosine esti-
L153: 
L154: mator (ACE) hav e been developed, which are mostly based on
L155: 
L156: different statistical hypotheses. The key to ha ving a satisfactory
L157: 
L158: detection result while adapting these classical algorithms is
L159: 
L160: the estimation of background characteristics, particularly the
L161: 
L162: background covariance. Howe ver, accurate background char-
L163: 
L164: acteristics are not easy to obtain from the primitive HSI due
L165: 
L166: to difﬁculties in eliminating the target pixels from the pool of

L193: estimation process, which is known as target contamination.
L194: 
L195: Many methods based on classical algorithms have been de-
L196: 
L197: veloped to mitigate the target contamination problem [1]–[6].
L198: 
L199: For example, a random selection method is used to reduce the
L200: 
L201: probability of target contamination [2], through which the target
L202: 
L203: contamination phenomenon can be well mitigated. A series
L204: 
L205: of multiple windows is used to exclude potential target pixels
L206: 
L207: [3]. However, prior information such as the size of the target
L208: and the nearest distance between two targets are still required.
L209: 
L210: Other approaches based on a global background [4] and a local
L211: 
L212: background [5] are aimed at the target contamination problem.
L213: 
L214: The impact of target contamination is also studied, which shows
L215: 
L216: that the degradation of TD accuracy cannot be ignored [7].
L217: 
L218: Recently, sparse representation has been already successfully
L219: 
L220: applied on classiﬁcation tasks [8], [9], and it also gives us a
L221: different view in hyperspectral TD [10]. A hyperspectral pixel
L222: 
L223: can be expressed as a linear combination of only a few elements
L224: 
L225: from a spectral dictionary, in which some are tar get spectrums
L226: 
L227: and the others belong to the background. The performance of
L228: 
L229: a sparse TD method mostly depends on the spectral dictionary.
L230: 
L231: It is common to build the dictionary upon prior global training
L232: 
L233: samples or a local background. Unless prior information such as
L234: training samples (enough target and background spectrums) or
L235: 
L236: the size of a local window (to exclude the target samples from
L237: 
L238: background samples) is acquired, the contamination problem
L239: 
L240: will still remain.
L241: 
L242: In order to reduce the occurrence of target contamination, we
L243: 
L244: introduce a sparse coding method into HSI to learn a dictionary
L245: 
L246: [11], and we propose an approach for hyperspectral TD based
L247: 
L248: on the learned dictionary (LD). There already exist many
L249: learning dictionaries such as the K-SVD method [12]. However,
L250: 
L251: these methods learn a dictionary from a limited number of
L252: 
L253: training samples, which might include target samples. As a
L254: 
L255: result, the target spectrum may be also learned in that case.
L256: 
L257: In comparison, the sparse coding method randomly selects a
L258: 
L259: real number of samples in each loop and approximates the
L260: 
L261: ideal dictionary in the gradient direction afterward. As target
L262: 
L263: samples are always small and only occupy very fe w pixels, they
L264: are much less likely to be chosen during the learning process.
L265: 
L266: Therefore, it is assumed that the spectrum of the target cannot
L267: 
L268: be learned, whereas the spectrum of the background, due to
L269: 
L270: its high occupation, can be therefore learned well during the
L271: 
L272: process. As a result, the LD can be viewed as the background
L273: 
L274: dictionary. Such an LD has been already applied in classiﬁ-
L275: 
L276: cation tasks [13]. By adapting the LD to sparse TD methods,
L277: 
L278: no prior information is required, and the target contamination
L279: problem can be well mitigated.
